In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, across five Old Testament books and Wisdom, so its basic sense is consistent but appears in varied settings. The wording can describe withdrawing, keeping distance, or stepping back. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L713307.explanation: Phathaia, also rendered Fathea, is a proper name belonging to a person. It is not a common word describing an action, quality, object, or idea, so its meaning is chiefly its identification of that individual. In the Greek LXX, this name occurs once, in Ezra 10:23. The available information identifies the name but does not provide the surrounding verse text or enough context to explain anything further about the person. Its precise significance in that passage therefore depends on reading the surrounding account.

word:lxx:L713390.explanation: Phaspha is a proper name, rendered also as “Fasfa.” It identifies a named individual or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 7:38. Since it is a name preserved in the biblical genealogical record, its meaning is primarily identification: it tells the reader who or what is being named, rather than describing a broader concept.

word:lxx:L713471.explanation: Phileō means to like or be fond of.

word:lxx:L713512.explanation: Phinō, also rendered Fino, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it refers to a named person or place according to the naming context. This name occurs twice in the Greek text, both times in Numbers 33:42–43. Since the surrounding verse text is not available here, the name’s precise referent in those verses cannot be identified more fully from the name alone.

word:lxx:L713624.explanation: This Greek Old Testament noun means “batch.” It refers to material or food considered together as one prepared quantity, rather than as separate pieces. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament, in Exodus and Numbers, so its basic sense is specific and concrete rather than broad or abstract. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains a batch or combined quantity.

word:lxx:L713682.explanation: Chalepos means fierce. It can also mean difficult.

word:lxx:L713750.explanation: Charran is the name of a place.

word:lxx:L713866.explanation: This Greek LXX word means “snow.” It names snow or describes something in relation to snow, functioning as an adjective in its sentences. The word appears eight times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, including Psalms, Isaiah, Lamentations, Daniel, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains consistent: snow as a natural substance or visible comparison.

word:lxx:L713927.explanation: Chouth, also rendered Khuth, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once, at 2 Kings 17:30, so its meaning is primarily its identity as a named person or place rather than a general descriptive word. The available wording preserves the name in two forms, “Chouth” and “Khuth.” Without the surrounding verse text, the specific person or place identified by the name cannot be explained further here.

word:lxx:L714049.explanation: This adjective describes something that can be felt by touch. It points to a tangible or perceptible quality rather than something merely imagined or understood inwardly. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Exodus 10:21. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains the same: something accessible to physical feeling.
